Gaming performance

CPU or GPU upgrade: which will improve your games?

Use repeatable game tests, resolution changes and frame-time data to decide whether your CPU or GPU needs an upgrade.

By PC Part Performance · September 18, 2026
On this pageStart with a target you can measureRecord a repeatable baselineReduce resolution and watch what changesRule out problems an upgrade will not fixCompare the full cost of the upgradeWatch the walkthroughSources
The short answer

Test the games and settings you use. If reducing resolution substantially improves frame rate, investigate the GPU; if it does not, check CPU-side limits and frame caps before choosing an upgrade.

Start with a target you can measure

Pick the games you care about, the resolution you use and the frame rate you want. A system that is fast enough for one game may struggle in another. The limiting component can also change between a quiet indoor scene and a busy multiplayer match.

Avoid choosing an upgrade from a universal bottleneck percentage. A useful test describes the game, settings and hardware configuration. Without that context, a single number says very little about the experience you will get.

Source: Intel: understanding gaming bottlenecks

Record a repeatable baseline

Use a built-in benchmark or repeat the same short route through a game. Keep the resolution, quality settings and background applications consistent. Run the test more than once so that a loading event or background task does not determine your conclusion.

Look beyond average FPS. A frame-time graph shows uneven delivery that an average can hide. Low-percentile results can help describe slower moments, but compare results from the same tool and method: different summaries do not always measure the same thing.

Reduce resolution and watch what changes

Lower the rendering resolution while keeping other settings as similar as possible. A substantial frame-rate improvement suggests that graphics rendering was an important limit in that test. That is a reason to investigate a faster GPU, or to adjust demanding graphics settings before spending money.

If performance barely changes, investigate the CPU side, frame-rate caps and other limits. This is a diagnostic clue, not proof by itself. CPU utilization averaged across every core can look low even when a game’s critical thread is busy. GPU utilization also needs context when a frame cap or synchronization setting is active.

Source: Intel: identifying CPU- and GPU-bound scenarios

Rule out problems an upgrade will not fix

Check for unexpected temperature or power limits, background downloads, driver issues and insufficient memory. Shader compilation and asset loading can also create stutters. A faster graphics card cannot guarantee that every hitch disappears.

Change one setting at a time and repeat the same test. Record what helped. If lowering textures improves a problematic scene, investigate memory pressure and the game’s requirements rather than assuming every quality setting has the same cost.

Compare the full cost of the upgrade

A CPU change may also require a motherboard or different RAM. A GPU upgrade may need a different power supply or more case clearance. Compare complete upgrade paths, not just the two headline component prices.

Use measured reviews of your games to narrow the shortlist. Our FPS page can help explore estimated scenarios, but those calculations are not measured benchmarks for your own machine. Finish with exact-model compatibility checks and tests that match your intended resolution.
